Lecture 20

Gaussian random vectors

Deck C, slides 9 to 19⏱ 35 min read✓ 9 practice problems
Solutions stay hidden until you click them.

Big picture. The normal distribution is the most important single distribution (the CLT of L18 explains why). This lecture builds its vector version, the multivariate Gaussian N(μ,Σ). The whole lecture rests on one idea:

every Gaussian vector is an affine function of independent standard normals:  X=AZ+μ.

From that one idea, and the L19 tools (CAX+b​=ACX​AT and the Jacobian), we get the density, the fact that linear maps keep vectors Gaussian, and the two properties that make Gaussians so useful: marginals and conditionals of a Gaussian vector are again Gaussian, with explicit formulas.

Part A: the slides

Slide 9/36: Recap

On the slide. We looked at n-length random vectors X, which are essentially multivariate random variables. Its CDF/pdf is simply the joint CDF/pdf of the components. E[X]=[E[X1​],…,E[Xn​]], and CX​ is the covariance matrix. Let Y=G(X) where G:Rn→Rn is continuous and invertible with continuous partial derivatives. Let H denote its inverse. Then fY​(y)=fX​(H(y))∣J∣ where J is the determinant of the Jacobian matrix. If Y=AX+b, then CY​=ACX​AT and

fY​(y)=∣det(A)∣1​fX​(A−1(y−b)).

All of this is proved in L19 (slides 4, 7 and 8). The last formula is the engine of this lecture: apply it with X replaced by a standard normal vector.

Slide 10/36: The standard normal vector

On the slide. An n-length random vector Z is called a standard normal vector if its components Zi​ are independent and standard normal. What is E[Z] and CZ​? Show that the pdf is given by

fZ​(z)=(2π)n/21​e−21​zTz.

The blue question. Each Zi​ has mean 0 and variance 1, and independent components have zero covariance. So

E[Z]=0,CZ​=In​  (the n×n identity).

The pdf. Independent components multiply:

fZ​(z)=i=1∏n​2π​1​e−zi2​/2=(2π)n/21​exp(−21​i=1∑n​zi2​)=(2π)n/21​e−21​zTz,

because zTz=z12​+⋯+zn2​=∥z∥2.

Worth noticing. fZ​ depends on z only through its length ∥z∥. So the density is the same in every direction: rotating a standard normal vector gives a standard normal vector again. (If Q is orthogonal, QQT=I, then QZ has covariance QIQT=I, and by slide 14 below it is again standard normal.)

Slide 11/36: Building general Gaussians from Z

On the slide. Now suppose X=AZ+μ. What is E[X] and CX​? E[X]=μ and CX​=AAT. Note that A can have dimension n×l, in which case Z is an l-length standard normal. What is fX​(x)?

Why. By L19 slides 2 and 4, E[X]=AE[Z]+μ=μ and CX​=ACZ​AT=AIAT=AAT.

The shape of A. A does not have to be square.

  • l<n (fewer sources of randomness than components): CX​=AAT has rank at most l, so it is singular. Then X lives on a lower-dimensional plane in Rn and has no joint pdf. Example: X=(Z,2Z) lies on the line x2​=2x1​. This is still a perfectly good Gaussian vector (a degenerate one). Last year's HW9 Q4 and Q6 (Part B) produce such vectors.
  • l=n with A invertible: the usual case, with a pdf (slide 12).

Slide 12/36: The multivariate Gaussian density

On the slide. What is fX​(x)?

fX​(x)=∣det(A)∣1​fZ​(A−1(x−μ))=(2π)n/2det(CX​)​1​e−21​(x−μ)TCX−1​(x−μ)

Henceforth we will use the notation Σ to represent CX​. Definition 1: X is multivariate Gaussian with mean vector μ and covariance matrix Σ (denoted by X∼N(μ,Σ)) if for some A and μ, it can be written as X=AZ+μ where Z is a standard normal vector and Σ=AAT.

Filling in the red step (A square and invertible). The first line is the affine formula of slide 9 with b=μ. Put v=x−μ. Two facts turn it into the second line.

The exponent. Using (A−1)T=(AT)−1 and (AT)−1A−1=(AAT)−1:

(A−1v)T(A−1v)=vT(AT)−1A−1v=vT(AAT)−1v=vTΣ−1v.

The constant. detΣ=det(A)det(AT)=(detA)2, so ∣detA∣=detΣ​.

Together:

fX​(x)=(2π)n/2detΣ​1​exp(−21​(x−μ)TΣ−1(x−μ))​

Reading the formula.

  • With n=1 and Σ=σ2 it is the familiar 2π​σ1​e−(x−μ)2/(2σ2). The vector formula replaces "divide by σ2" with "multiply by Σ−1".
  • The density depends on A only through Σ=AAT. Many matrices give the same Σ (for example A and AQ for any orthogonal Q), and they all give the same distribution. So the notation N(μ,Σ) makes sense: a Gaussian vector is completely determined by its mean vector and covariance matrix.
  • The formula needs Σ invertible (detΣ>0). The degenerate case of slide 11 is covered by Definition 1 but has no pdf.
  • Check with L19 slide 1: X=(Z1​,Z1​+Z2​) has A=[11​01​], Σ=[11​12​], detΣ=1, Σ−1=[2−1​−11​]. The boxed formula gives 2π1​e−21​(2x12​−2x1​x2​+x22​), the same as the Jacobian answer there. ✓

Slide 13/36: Three equivalent definitions

On the slide. The following are equivalent definitions (without proof):

  1. X∼N(μ,Σ) if for some A and μ, it can be written as X=AZ+μ.
  2. X∼N(μ,Σ) if it has the pdf fX​(x)=(2π)n/2det(Σ)​1​e−21​(x−μ)TΣ−1(x−μ).
  3. X∼N(μ,Σ) iff for all vectors a∈Rn, it turns out that aTX is univariate Gaussian N(aTμ,aTΣa).

For equivalent definitions see https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multivariate_normal_distribution

How to use each one.

Definition Use it to...
1. X=AZ+μ build or simulate a Gaussian vector; prove things by reducing to independent Z's
2. the pdf compute probabilities and conditional densities; recognise a Gaussian by the form of its density
3. every linear combination is normal check that something is (or is not) a Gaussian vector; get the distribution of any aTX at once

Definition 3 is the one in last year's HW9 Q2 and Tutorial 9 Q3 ("X and Y are bivariate normal if aX+bY is normal for all a and b"). It counts a constant as a normal with variance 0, and it is the most useful in exams: for example X1​−3X2​+X3​∼N(aTμ,aTΣa) with a=(1,−3,1)T, with no integration at all.

Why they agree (sketch, not needed for the exam).

  • (1 ⇒ 3) aTX=(ATa)TZ+aTμ is a linear combination of independent normals plus a constant, so it is normal (L14 slide 5, by MGFs). Its mean and variance follow from L19.
  • (1 ⇒ 2) This is slide 12, when A is invertible.
  • (2 ⇒ 1) Take A=Σ1/2, the symmetric square root, and check with the Jacobian that Z=A−1(X−μ) has the pdf of slide 10.
  • (3 ⇒ 1) By definition 3, sTX is normal for every s, so the multivariate MGF is E[esTX]=esTμ+21​sTΣs (slide 14 below). That is also the MGF of AZ+μ for any A with AAT=Σ. Equal MGFs give equal distributions.

Slide 14/36: Affine maps preserve Gaussianity

On the slide. Suppose X∼N(μ,Σ); then what can we say about Y=AX+b? Is it a Gaussian vector? Easy to see that E[Y]=AE[X]+b and CY​=AΣAT. Like in the univariate case, we can use MGF (for multivariate MGF see Bertsekas) to show the following. Suppose X∼N(μ,Σ). Now consider Y=AX+b. Then we have Y∼N(AE[X]+b,AΣAT).

X∼N(μ,Σ) ⟹ AX+b∼N(Aμ+b, AΣAT)​

The mean and covariance come free from L19. The new content is that Y is still Gaussian. Here is the MGF proof the slide points to. It is last year's HW9 Q10 and Tutorial 9 Q4.

The multivariate MGF. For a random vector, MX​(s)=E[esTX] for s∈Rn. Just as in L14, if it is finite near s=0 it determines the joint distribution (Bertsekas Section 4.4, transforms of joint distributions).

Step 1 (HW9 Q10): the MGF of N(μ,Σ). Write X=AZ+μ and put u=ATs. Then sTX=uTZ+sTμ, and by independence and the 1D normal MGF E[euZ]=eu2/2:

MX​(s)=esTμi∏​E[eui​Zi​]=esTμe21​∑i​ui2​=esTμ+21​uTu.

Since uTu=sTAATs=sTΣs:

MX​(s)=exp(sTμ+21​sTΣs)​

(This is the 1D formula eμt+σ2t2/2 with t replaced by the vector s.)

Step 2 (Tutorial 9 Q4): the MGF of Y=AX+b. Since sTY=(ATs)TX+sTb,

MY​(s)=esTbMX​(ATs)=exp(sT(Aμ+b)+21​sT(AΣAT)s).

This is the MGF of N(Aμ+b,AΣAT), so by uniqueness that is the distribution of Y. □

A can be any m×n matrix here. Taking A to be a row vector aT gives definition 3 of slide 13. Taking A to pick out some of the coordinates gives the marginalization property of the next slide.

Slide 15/36: Marginalization and conditioning

On the slide. Let X∼N(μ,Σ) and partition X as [X1​,X2​]T, where X1​ is m×1 and X2​ is (n−m)×1. We similarly have μ=[μ1​,μ2​]T and Σ=[Σ11​Σ21​​Σ12​Σ22​​], where Σ11​ is an m×m matrix and so on. Marginalization property: the m-dimensional marginal distribution of X1​ is N(μ1​,Σ11​) and X2​ is N(μ2​,Σ22​). Conditioning property: the m-dimensional conditional distribution of X1​ given X2​=x2​ is

N(μ1​+Σ12​Σ22−1​(x2​−μ2​), Σ11​−Σ12​Σ22−1​Σ21​).

Note the decrease in variance, which does not depend on x2​.

The slide says "without proof"; here are both proofs, since the second is last year's Tutorial 9 Q6.

Marginalization. X1​=[Im​  0]X. By slide 14 it is Gaussian with mean [Im​  0]μ=μ1​ and covariance [Im​  0]Σ[Im​  0]T=Σ11​. In words: to get a marginal, just delete the rows and columns of the other variables. For example, if X∼N(μ,Σ) in R3, then X2​∼N(μ2​,Σ22​) and (X1​,X3​) has mean (μ1​,μ3​) and covariance [Σ11​Σ31​​Σ13​Σ33​​] (entries of the 3×3 matrix).

Conditioning: the "remove what X2​ explains" proof. Let B=Σ12​Σ22−1​ and define the residual

W=X1​−BX2​.
  1. (W,X2​) is a Gaussian vector, since it is a linear function of X (slide 14).
  2. W and X2​ are uncorrelated: Cov(W,X2​)=Σ12​−BΣ22​=Σ12​−Σ12​=0.
  3. So they are independent. For a Gaussian vector, zero cross-covariance makes the MGF factor: with block-diagonal covariance, exp(s1T​μW​+s2T​μ2​+21​s1T​ΣW​s1​+21​s2T​Σ22​s2​)=MW​(s1​)MX2​​(s2​), which is the MGF of an independent pair.
  4. Mean and covariance of W: E[W]=μ1​−Bμ2​, and expanding Cov(X1​−BX2​),
ΣW​=Σ11​−BΣ21​−Σ12​BT+BΣ22​BT=Σ11​−Σ12​Σ22−1​Σ21​,

since the last three terms are each Σ12​Σ22−1​Σ21​ (using Σ21​=Σ12T​ and Σ22​ symmetric). 5. Condition. X1​=W+BX2​. Given X2​=x2​, the term Bx2​ is a constant and W keeps its distribution (it is independent of X2​). So

X1​∣X2​=x2​ ∼ N(μ1​−Bμ2​+Bx2​, ΣW​)=N(μ1​+Σ12​Σ22−1​(x2​−μ2​), Σ11​−Σ12​Σ22−1​Σ21​). □

Reading the formula.

  • The conditional mean is linear in x2​. It starts at the prior mean μ1​ and moves by Σ12​Σ22−1​ times the "surprise" x2​−μ2​. With one variable each, this is μ1​+σ22​σ12​​(x2​−μ2​), the regression line.
  • The conditional covariance is smaller (we subtract the PSD matrix Σ12​Σ22−1​Σ21​). Observing X2​ reduces our uncertainty about X1​.
  • The note on the slide: the reduction is the same whatever value x2​ we observe. This is special to Gaussians. For most other joint distributions, the conditional variance depends on the observed value.
  • If Σ12​=0, then X1​∣X2​∼N(μ1​,Σ11​), the marginal: uncorrelated parts of a Gaussian vector are independent.

Slide 16/36: Towards bivariate Gaussians

On the slide. Suppose X1​∼N(μ1​,σ12​) and X2​∼N(μ2​,σ22​). Also suppose X1​ and X2​ are independent. For x=[x1​,x2​]T [the slide prints [x2​,x2​]T], we have

fX​(x)=fX1​​(x1​)fX2​​(x2​)=2πσ1​σ2​1​e−(2σ12​(x1​−μ1​)2​+2σ22​(x2​−μ2​)2​)=(2π)det(Σ)​1​e−21​(x−μ)TΣ−1(x−μ)

where Σ=[σ12​0​0σ22​​], and hence X is bivariate Gaussian. In general, a vector composed of independent Gaussians is a Gaussian vector. The converse is not true: a vector of dependent Gaussian components need not be a Gaussian vector (EX 5.35 in probabilitycourse.com).

Checking the last equality. detΣ=σ12​σ22​, so detΣ​=σ1​σ2​. And Σ−1=diag(1/σ12​,1/σ22​), so

21​(x−μ)TΣ−1(x−μ)=2σ12​(x1​−μ1​)2​+2σ22​(x2​−μ2​)2​. ✓

This matches the pdf of slide 13 with n=2, so X is a Gaussian vector.

The counterexample: Gaussian components, but not a Gaussian vector (probabilitycourse 5.3.2; the slide calls it EX 5.35). Let X∼N(0,1) and, independently, flip a fair coin W. Set Y=X on heads and Y=−X on tails.

  • Y∼N(0,1): conditioning on the coin, FY​(y)=21​Φ(y)+21​P(−X≤y)=21​Φ(y)+21​Φ(y)=Φ(y), since −X∼N(0,1) too.
  • But X+Y is 2X on heads and 0 on tails. So P(X+Y=0)=21​: not a normal distribution (a normal with positive variance gives probability 0 to a point, and X+Y is not a constant either). Definition 3 fails with a=(1,1), so (X,Y) is not a Gaussian vector.
  • Also Cov(X,Y)=E[XY]=21​E[X2]−21​E[X2]=0. So X,Y are uncorrelated and each normal, yet clearly dependent (∣Y∣=∣X∣ always).

The lesson: "uncorrelated implies independent" holds for jointly Gaussian variables (slide 15), not merely for variables that are each Gaussian. Exam questions test exactly this.

Slide 17/36: Bivariate Gaussians

On the slide. In general, X1​ and X2​ need not be independent, in which case we have a general bivariate Gaussian X=[X1​,X2​]T∼N(μ,Σ), where μ=[μ1​,μ2​]T and Σ=[σ11​σ21​​σ12​σ22​​]. Show that bivariate Gaussian is closed under marginalization, i.e., X1​∼N(μ1​,σ11​) and X2​∼N(μ2​,σ22​). Show that bivariate Gaussian is closed under conditioning (for proof see Theorem 5.4, probabilitycourse.com). This means that given X2​=x2​, one can show that fX1​∣X2​​(x1​∣x2​) is Gaussian. These two properties make multivariate Gaussians efficient modelling tools and handy in Gaussian processes and Bayesian optimization.

The bivariate density written out. Write σ11​=σ12​, σ22​=σ22​ and σ12​=σ21​=ρσ1​σ2​, where ρ is the correlation coefficient, −1<ρ<1. Then

detΣ=σ12​σ22​(1−ρ2),Σ−1=σ12​σ22​(1−ρ2)1​[σ22​−ρσ1​σ2​​−ρσ1​σ2​σ12​​]

(the 2×2 inverse: swap the diagonal, negate the off-diagonal, divide by the determinant). With u=σ1​x1​−μ1​​ and v=σ2​x2​−μ2​​ (standardised values), the pdf of slide 13 becomes

f(x1​,x2​)=2πσ1​σ2​1−ρ2​1​exp(−2(1−ρ2)u2−2ρuv+v2​)​

With μ=0 and σ1​=σ2​=1, it is the formula quoted in last year's HW9 Q2 and Tutorial 9 Q3.

Both red questions at once: complete the square. Since u2−2ρuv+v2=(1−ρ2)u2+(v−ρu)2,

f(x1​,x2​)=pdf of N(μ1​,σ12​) at x1​2π​σ1​1​e−u2/2​​ × pdf of N(μ2​+ρσ2​u, (1−ρ2)σ22​) at x2​2π​σ2​1−ρ2​1​exp(−2(1−ρ2)(v−ρu)2​)​​.

(Check the second factor: 1−ρ2(v−ρu)2​=(1−ρ2)σ22​(x2​−μ2​−ρσ2​u)2​.)

  • Marginalization. Integrate over x2​: the second factor is a pdf in x2​, so it integrates to 1, leaving $f_{X_1}(x_1) = $ the N(μ1​,σ12​) pdf, that is, X1​∼N(μ1​,σ11​). By symmetry (complete the square in u instead), X2​∼N(μ2​,σ22​).
  • Conditioning. fX2​∣X1​​(x2​∣x1​)=fX1​​(x1​)f(x1​,x2​)​ is exactly the second factor:
X2​∣X1​=x1​ ∼ N(μ2​+ρσ2​σ1​x1​−μ1​​, (1−ρ2)σ22​)(probabilitycourse Theorem 5.4).

Swapping the roles of the two variables,

X1​∣X2​=x2​ ∼ N(μ1​+ρσ1​σ2​x2​−μ2​​, (1−ρ2)σ12​)​

This is slide 15 with Σ12​Σ22−1​=σ22​ρσ1​σ2​​=σ2​ρσ1​​ and Σ11​−Σ22​Σ122​​=σ12​−ρ2σ12​. ✓

How to remember the conditional. In standard units: if X2​ is v standard deviations above its mean, the best guess for X1​ is ρv standard deviations above its mean ("regression to the mean" when ∣ρ∣<1). The remaining spread is σ1​1−ρ2​. At ρ=0, observing X2​ tells us nothing. As ∣ρ∣→1, it tells us almost everything.

The constructive view (probabilitycourse 5.3.2, Theorem 5.3). Every bivariate normal can be written as

X1​=μ1​+σ1​Z1​,X2​=μ2​+σ2​(ρZ1​+1−ρ2​Z2​),

with Z1​,Z2​ independent N(0,1). This is definition 1 with A=[σ1​ρσ2​​0σ2​1−ρ2​​]; check that AAT=Σ. It is how Tutorial 9 Q3 is usually answered: this pair has the right means, variances and correlation, every aX1​+bX2​ is normal, and a Gaussian vector is fixed by its mean and covariance. The Jacobian (Z1​=U, Z2​=1−ρ2​V−ρU​ in standard units, so ∣J∣=1−ρ2​1​) then gives the boxed pdf.

Gaussian processes and Bayesian optimization (context only, not exam material). A Gaussian process models an unknown function f by declaring that the values (f(t1​),…,f(tk​)) at any finite set of points form a Gaussian vector. After measuring f at a few points, the conditioning formula of slide 15 gives, in closed form, a prediction (the conditional mean) and an uncertainty (the conditional variance) at every other point. Bayesian optimization uses these to choose where to measure next. Both rely only on the two closure properties of this slide.

Slides 18 and 19/36: Pictures of bivariate Gaussian pdfs

On the slides. Slide 18: a 3-D plot of a bell-shaped joint density p(x,y) over the (x,y) plane, with the two marginal densities p(x) and p(y) drawn as curves on the back walls. Slide 19: a cloud of simulated points from a bivariate Gaussian, with a green ellipse around the bulk of the cloud, and histograms of each coordinate on the back walls with the marginal pdfs (red and blue curves) drawn over them.

What to see in them.

  1. The marginals are normal curves (slide 17's marginalization), on both slides. On slide 19 the histograms of each coordinate of the simulated points match the normal pdfs drawn over them.
  2. The marginal curves can have different heights. A normal pdf peaks at 2π​σ1​, so the taller, narrower marginal belongs to the coordinate with the smaller variance.
  3. The contours are ellipses. The density is constant where (x−μ)TΣ−1(x−μ)=c, which is an ellipse centred at μ, like the green curve on slide 19. With ρ=0 its axes are parallel to the coordinate axes (a circle if also σ1​=σ2​). With ρ=0 it is tilted: for ρ>0 the cloud leans along a rising line, for ρ<0 along a falling line. In general its axes point along the eigenvectors of Σ, with half-lengths proportional to the square roots of the eigenvalues.
  4. How much probability an ellipse holds is worked out in B12 below: the "2-standard-deviation" ellipse (c=4) holds only about 86%, not the 95% of the 1-D rule.

Part B: extra worked examples and problems

B1 (last year's HW9 Q4). X∼N(m,C) with m=[12​], C=[41​11​]. Let Y=AX+b with A=​2−11​113​​ and b=​−101​​. Find (a) P(X2​>0), (b) mY​, (c) CY​, (d) P(Y2​≤2).

Solution

Solution. (a) By marginalization X2​∼N(2,1), so P(X2​>0)=P(Z>10−2​)=Φ(2)≈0.9772. (b) mY​=Am+b=(4,1,7)+(−1,0,1)=(3,1,8)T. (c) AC=​9−37​304​​, and multiplying by AT:

CY​=ACAT=​21−618​−63−3​18−319​​.

(d) By slide 14, Y2​=−X1​+X2​∼N(1,3), so P(Y2​≤2)=Φ(3​1​)=Φ(0.577)≈0.7181. Remark. Y is 3-dimensional but built from the 2-dimensional X, so CY​ is singular (detCY​=0). Y is a degenerate Gaussian vector with no joint pdf in R3, yet every component is a normal variable (slide 11).

B2 (last year's HW9 Q5). X=(X1​,X2​,X3​)∼N(μ,Σ) with μ=(1,2,3)T and Σ=​410​121​013​​. Find the distribution of (X1​,X3​) given X2​=x2​.

Solution

Solution. Take X1​=(X1​,X3​) (the part we want) and X2​=X2​ (the part we observe). Reading off the entries:

Σ11​=[40​03​],Σ12​=[11​],Σ22​=2.

Then Σ12​Σ22−1​=[1/21/2​], and

μ1∣2​=[13​]+2x2​−2​[11​],Σ1∣2​=[40​03​]−21​[11​11​]=[3.5−0.5​−0.52.5​].

Notice: X1​ and X3​ are uncorrelated (independent) to begin with, but given X2​ they become negatively correlated. Both are positively tied to X2​, so once X2​ is known, a high X1​ "uses up" some of what X2​ explains and points to a lower X3​.

B3 (last year's HW9 Q6): a degenerate Gaussian. Z=(Z1​,Z2​)∼N(m,C) with m=(1,2)T and C=[2−1​−13​]. Let W=AZ+b with A=​112​1−10​​, b=(0,0,−2)T. (a) Find the mean and covariance of W. (b) Find P(W2​>1).

Solution

Solution. (Here Z is not standard normal; it is just the name of the vector.) (a) E[W]=Am+b=(3,−1,2)+(0,0,−2)=(3,−1,0)T. Next, AC=​134​2−4−2​​, so

CW​=ACAT=​3−12​−176​268​​.

Spot checks: Var(W2​)=Var(Z1​−Z2​)=2+3−2(−1)=7 and Var(W3​)=Var(2Z1​)=8. ✓ As in B1, detCW​=0 (rank 2). (b) W2​∼N(−1,7), so P(W2​>1)=1−Φ(7​1−(−1)​)=1−Φ(0.756)≈0.2248.

B4 (last year's HW9 Q2). (X,Y) is standard bivariate normal with correlation ρ (pdf in slide 17). Find the joint pdf of U=X+Y and V=X−Y.

Solution 1 (the fast way, slide 14). (U,V) is a linear image of a Gaussian vector, so it is Gaussian, with

Var(U)=2+2ρ,Var(V)=2−2ρ,Cov(U,V)=Var(X)−Var(Y)=0.

Uncorrelated parts of a Gaussian vector are independent, so U∼N(0,2(1+ρ)) and V∼N(0,2(1−ρ)) are independent:

fU,V​(u,v)=4π1−ρ2​1​exp(−4(1+ρ)u2​−4(1−ρ)v2​).

Solution 2 (the Jacobian, L19). x=2u+v​, y=2u−v​, ∣J∣=21​, and x2−2ρxy+y2=2(1−ρ)u2+(1+ρ)v2​. Substituting into the pdf gives the same answer.

B5 (last year's HW9 Q11). X is a standard normal vector in Rn and Y=AX+b, with A square, symmetric and invertible. (a) Find fY​. (b) Evaluate it for A=[20​03​], b=(1,−1)T, y=(3,2)T.

Solution

Solution. (a) By slide 12 with Σ=AAT=A2:

fY​(y)=(2π)n/2∣detA∣1​exp(−21​(y−b)TA−2(y−b))=(2π)n/2∣detA∣1​exp(−21​​A−1(y−b)​2).

(b) A−1(y−b)=(22​,33​)=(1,1), with squared length 2, and detA=6. So fY​(y)=2π⋅61​e−1=12πe−1​≈0.00976.

B6 (last year's Tutorial 9 Q5). X∼N(0,[52​21​]). Find a such that Y1​=X1​+aX2​ and Y2​=X2​ are independent.

Solution

Solution. (Y1​,Y2​) is a linear image of X, hence Gaussian, so independence is the same as zero covariance: Cov(X1​+aX2​,X2​)=2+a⋅1=0, so a=−2. In general a=−σ22​σ12​​: Y1​ is the residual W of the slide-15 proof. Here Var(Y1​)=5+4−4⋅2=1, so X1​=Y1​+2X2​ and X1​∣X2​=x2​∼N(2x2​,1), exactly as the conditioning formula says.

B7 (probabilitycourse 5.3.2, numerical example). X,Y are bivariate normal with μX​=1, σX2​=1, μY​=0, σY2​=4, ρ=21​. Find (a) P(2X+Y≤3), (b) Cov(X+Y,2X−Y), (c) P(Y>1∣X=2).

Solution

Solution. Cov(X,Y)=ρσX​σY​=1. (a) V=2X+Y is normal with mean 2 and variance 4⋅1+4+2⋅2⋅1=12, so P(V≤3)=Φ(12​1​)≈0.6136. (b) By bilinearity, 2Var(X)−Cov(X,Y)+2Cov(Y,X)−Var(Y)=2−1+2−4=−1. (c) Y∣X=2 is normal with mean 0+21​⋅2⋅12−1​=1 and variance (1−41​)⋅4=3, so P(Y>1∣X=2)=1−Φ(0)=21​.

B8 (Bertsekas Chapter 4, Problem 28): the bivariate normal from scratch. The zero-mean bivariate normal pdf is f(x,y)=ce−q(x,y) with

q(x,y)=2(1−ρ2)σx2​x2​−2ρσx​σy​xy​+σy2​y2​​,−1<ρ<1.

(a) Write q as (αx−βy)2+γ2y2. (b) Show X∼N(0,σx2​) and Y∼N(0,σy2​). (c) Find c. (d) Find the conditional pdf of X given Y=y. (e) Show the correlation coefficient is ρ. (f) Show X,Y are independent iff uncorrelated. (g) Show the estimation error E[X∣Y]−X is normal with mean 0 and variance (1−ρ2)σx2​, and independent of Y.

Solution

Solution. (a) Completing the square in x (as in slide 17):

q=2(1−ρ2)(σx​x​−ρσy​y​)2​+2σy2​y2​,soα=σx​2(1−ρ2)​1​,  β=σy​2(1−ρ2)​ρ​,  γ=2​σy​1​.

(b) ∫e−(αx−βy)2dx=απ​​ for every y, so fY​(y)=αcπ​​e−y2/(2σy2​), a N(0,σy2​) shape. By symmetry, X∼N(0,σx2​). (c) Matching fY​ to 2π​σy​1​e−y2/(2σy2​): c=π​2π​σy​α​=2πσx​σy​1−ρ2​1​. (d) fX∣Y​(x∣y)∝e−(αx−βy)2=exp(−2(1−ρ2)σx2​(x−ρσy​σx​​y)2​), so X∣Y=y∼N(ρσy​σx​​y, (1−ρ2)σx2​). (e) E[XY]=E[YE[X∣Y]]=ρσy​σx​​E[Y2]=ρσx​σy​, so the correlation coefficient is σx​σy​ρσx​σy​​=ρ. (f) Independent always implies uncorrelated. Conversely, uncorrelated means ρ=0, and then q=2σx2​x2​+2σy2​y2​, so the pdf factors. (g) Given Y=y, the error E[X∣Y]−X=ρσy​σx​​y−X is, by (d), N(0,(1−ρ2)σx2​) whatever y is. A conditional distribution that does not depend on y means the error is independent of Y, and that is also its unconditional distribution.

B9 (an illustrative example; the numbers are made up). Heights (cm) of two siblings are bivariate normal, with μ1​=170, σ1​=7 for the younger and μ2​=175, σ2​=8 for the older, and ρ=0.5. The older sibling is 183 cm. What is the chance the younger one is over 180 cm?

Solution

Solution. By slide 17, X1​∣X2​=183 is normal with

mean 170+0.5⋅87​(183−175)=173.5,SD 71−0.25​≈6.062.

So P(X1​>180∣X2​=183)=1−Φ(6.062180−173.5​)=1−Φ(1.072)≈0.142. Without the information, P(X1​>180)=1−Φ(10/7)≈0.077: knowing a tall sibling nearly doubles the chance. The older sibling is 1 SD above average, and the prediction for the younger moves only ρ×1=0.5 SD above average.

B10: simulating any bivariate normal (probabilitycourse 5.3.2, Eq. 5.23, together with Box–Muller from L19 B11).

  1. Make Z1​,Z2​ independent N(0,1) from two uniforms by Box–Muller.
  2. Find A with AAT=Σ. For 2×2, the lower-triangular choice (the Cholesky factor) is A=[σ1​ρσ2​​0σ2​1−ρ2​​].
  3. Return X=AZ+μ (definition 1).

Example. Σ=[42​25​]: σ1​=2, ρσ2​=σ1​σ12​​=1, σ2​1−ρ2​=5−1​=2, so A=[21​02​]; check AAT=[42​25​]. ✓ With μ=(1,0) and Z=(0.5,−1), the sample is X=(1+1, 0.5−2)=(2,−1.5).

In code, for any dimension:

import numpy as np
L = np.linalg.cholesky(Sigma)            # lower triangular, L @ L.T == Sigma
Z = np.random.standard_normal((N, len(mu)))
X = mu + Z @ L.T                         # each row is one sample of N(mu, Sigma)
print(np.cov(X, rowvar=False))           # close to Sigma for large N

B11: Gaussian vector or not? Decide for each pair; X,Z are independent N(0,1).

  1. (X,3X+1). Yes (definition 1 with A=[1,3]T), but degenerate: all its mass is on a line, with no joint pdf.
  2. (X+Z,X−Z). Yes, a linear image of the standard normal vector (X,Z); in fact two independent N(0,2) variables (B4 with ρ=0).
  3. (X,Y) with Y=X or −X on a fair coin flip. No (slide 16).
  4. (X,Y) with Y=∣Z∣sign(X). Y∼N(0,1), because ∣Z∣ gets a random sign independent of it. But X and Y always have the same sign, so P(X>0,Y<0)=0. A non-degenerate bivariate normal has a positive pdf everywhere, so it gives that quadrant positive probability. A degenerate one lies on a line through the origin; Y=cX is impossible here, because given X, Y still varies. No.
  5. (X,X2). No: X2 is not even normal.

B12: how much probability is inside an ellipse? Let X∼N(μ,Σ) in R2 with Σ invertible. Find P((X−μ)TΣ−1(X−μ)≤c).

Solution

Solution. Write X=AZ+μ. By the slide-12 calculation, the quadratic form equals ZTZ=Z12​+Z22​. Box–Muller (L19 B11) says Z12​+Z22​=R2=−2lnU for a uniform U. So

P(Z12​+Z22​≤c)=P(U≥e−c/2)=1−e−c/2,

that is, Z12​+Z22​∼ Exponential with rate 21​. For the "2-SD ellipse" (c=4) this is 1−e−2≈0.865. The ellipse holding 95% has c=−2ln0.05≈5.99. (In n dimensions, ZTZ has the chi-square distribution with n degrees of freedom; you meet it again in statistics.)
